## Activity

![](qr-code.png)


## What are (word) embeddings?
::: {.fragment}
Word embeddings are dense vector representations of words that capture semantic meaning.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Words with similar meanings are placed close to each other in a multi-dimensional space.
:::

## BOW vs Embeddings

Bag-of-Words:

```text
cat = [1, 0, 0, 0, 0, ..., 0]  (10,000 dimensions)
dog = [0, 1, 0, 0, 0, ..., 0]
car = [0, 0, 1, 0, 0, ..., 0]
```

- Each word is an isolated symbol, no "meaning" encoded

- "cat" and "dog" are just as different as "cat" and "car"

- Sparse vectors: thousands of dimensions, mostly zeros

- Dimensions = vocabulary size

## BOW vs Embeddings

::: {.fragment}
How do we associate a word with a meaning (e.g., a cognitive process, an emotion)?
:::

::: {.fragment}
Core idea: Words appearing in similar contexts have similar meanings.

> "You shall know a word by the company it keeps"
> — J.R. Firth (1957)
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-note}
Similarity comes from shared context, not co-occurrence
:::
:::

:::{.fragment}
Distributional Semantic Models (DSMs) = algorithms that learn the meanings of tokens (or at least the relations between their meanings) from patterns of contextual co-occurrence
:::

## Why embeddings matter

::: {.fragment}
```text
cat  = [0.2, -0.4, 0.7, ..., 0.1]  (300 dimensions)  
dog  = [0.3, -0.5, 0.8, ..., 0.2]  (similar to cat!)  
car  = [-0.1, 0.6, -0.3, ..., 0.4] (different from cat/dog) 
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
Advantages:

- Semantic similarity captured

- Dense, efficient representation

- Fixed dimensions (typically 256-4096)

- Mathematical operations meaningful
:::

## Applications

::: {.fragment}
Real-World Applications

- Search engines & information retrieval — go beyond keyword matching

- Machine translation — map meaning across languages

- Sentiment analysis & text classification — richer features than raw words

- Question answering & recommendation systems — match by meaning, not just form

- Named entity recognition — recognize entities in context
:::

::: {.fragment}
Linguistic Research

- Semantic change — track how word meanings shift across decades

- Bias detection — uncover implicit associations (e.g. gender, race)

- Metaphor analysis — identify non-literal and cross-domain mappings

- Construct representation — extract constructs from word vectors
:::

## Navigating the vector space

::: {.fragment}
Embeddings represent words as vectors in high-dimensional space where:
:::

- Each dimension captures some aspect of meaning
- Similar words cluster together
- Relationships are preserved geometrically

::: {.fragment}
We can quantify similarity between vectors:

Euclidean distance
: Straight-line distance
: Low = similar

Cosine similarity
: Angle between vectors
: 1 = identical, -1 = opposite

Dot product
: Angle + magnitude
: Higher = more similar and prominent
:::

## Types of word embeddings

::: {.fragment}
Count-based methods (e.g., LSA, HAL)
:::

::: {.fragment}
DFM -> Find patterns of co-occurrence -> Reduce dimensionality
:::

::: {.fragment}
Advantages:
:::

- Straightforward to understand

- Interpretable dimensions

- Good for small datasets

::: {.fragment}
Disadvantages:
:::

- Uses documents to define word contexts

- Assumes linearity and normality

- Less effective than modern methods

- Same problems with raw word counts

## Types of word embeddings

::: {.fragment}
Prediction-Based Methods (e.g., GloVe^\[1\]^, word2vec^\[2\]^, fastText^\[3\]^)

The model weights are the embeddings
:::

::: {.fragment}
Two main architectures:
:::

CBOW

: Input: Context words

: Output: Target word

: Fast training

: Better for frequent words

Skip-gram

: Input: Target word

: Output: Context words

: Slower training

: Better for rare words and small datasets

## Types of decontextualized embeddings

::: {.fragment}
Word2vec:
:::
- efficient 

- two vectors per word 

- struggles with polisemy

- works better with English

::: {.fragment}
GloVe:
:::

- better trained models than Word2Vec

- same issues than Word2vec

::: {.fragment}
FastText:
:::

- works with shingles rather than words

- can infer embeddings of "absent" words

- more complex (larger models)


## Types of word embeddings

::: {.fragment}
Contextualized embeddings (e.g., BERT^\[1\]^, RoBERTa^\[2\]^, SBERT^\[3\]^)

Different embeddings for different contexts (with transformers)
:::

::: {.fragment}
1. Input text → converted to static word embeddings (like Word2Vec/GloVe)

2. Embeddings → transformer layers identify connections between words

3. Connections → embeddings are shifted to reflect context ("short circuit" → electrical meaning)

4. Repeated across many layers → progressively richer representations

5. Final embeddings → used for the target task (next word prediction, classification, etc.)
:::

## Types of contextualized embeddings

::: {.fragment}
BERT
:::

- generalize to many tasks

- reliable

- [CLS] as summary of text

::: {.fragment}
RoBERTa
:::

- focus on author-level characteristics (e.g., age, gender, personality)

- larger and longer training

::: {.fragment}
SBERT
:::

- sentence-level embeddings

- guarantees geometrical properties


## Visualizing the vector space

::: {.fragment}
Word vectors live in 300 dimensions — impossible to visualize directly.

Dimensionality reduction projects them into 2D while preserving structure.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Three common methods:
:::

PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
: Finds the directions of maximum variance globally
: Preserves global structure — clusters that are far apart stay far apart
: Fast, deterministic, but misses local non-linear structure

t-SNE
: Handles non-linear structure better
: Excellent at revealing tight local clusters
: Slow, non-deterministic, distorts global distances — two clusters being far apart means nothing

UMAP
: Similar intuition to t-SNE but preserves both local and some global structure
: Faster than t-SNE, more stable across runs
: Best general-purpose choice for word embeddings

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-warning}
These methods show structure that was already in the 300D space — they don't create similarity, they reveal it.
:::
:::


## À la carte (ALC) embeddings

::: {.fragment}
The problem with decontextualized embeddings: "lula" has one fixed vector.
:::

::: {.fragment}
ALC embeddings builds a context-specific vector for a target word:

1. Take every occurrence of the target word in your corpus
2. Collect the words in a window around each occurrence (e.g. ±6 words)
3. Average their pretrained GloVe vectors
4. Multiply by a learned transformation matrix to align the result with the GloVe space
:::

::: {.fragment}
The result: one embedding per instance of the word, not per word type.

You can then average across groups to get "what does this word mean for group A vs group B?"
:::


## conText — nearest neighbors by group

::: {.fragment}
[`conText`](https://github.com/prodriguezsosa/conText/tree/master) operationalizes this for social science:

- Pick a target word (e.g. "lula", "vacina", "fraude")
- Define a grouping variable (e.g. misinformation label, party, time period)
- Get the top N nearest neighbors of that word's ALC embedding separately for each group
- Compare: what words does each group associate with the target?
:::

::: {.fragment}
Does this word mean different things to different groups?
